results.title: Sim-To-Real: Uniting Simulation And Reality for Unprecedented Results
results.content: By aligning simulated environments with real-world conditions, this approach enhances the robustness and applicability of virtual training systems.** These systems play a crucial role in fields like robotics, autonomous vehicles, and computer vision as they simulate various scenarios, allowing for testing and training without the need for physical prototypes. Sim-to-real techniques employ domain adaptation, transfer learning, and reinforcement learning algorithms to adapt simulated training models to real-world data, providing more accurate and reliable results. Sim-To-Real: Bridging The Gap Between Simulation And Reality ### Simulation Vs. Reality: Understanding The Differences Simulations have long been used to recreate real-world scenarios in a controlled environment. Domain Adaptation: Adapting Simulated Environments To Real-World Scenarios The field of sim-to-real has seen significant advancements in recent years, providing exciting opportunities to bridge the gap between simulation and reality. Reinforcement Learning: Training Agents In Realistic Environments ### Sim-To-Real – Bridging The Gap Between Simulation And Reality Reinforcement learning (rl) is a powerful technique in the field of machine learning that enables agents to learn and improve their behavior through trial and error. Robotics: Advancing Autonomous Systems Through Realistic Simulations * Simulated robot movements allow researchers and engineers to test and refine their algorithms in a virtual environment before deploying them in the real world. * By accurately replicating real-world scenarios, simulations allow developers to train robots in complex tasks and challenging environments. By simulating robot movements, fine-tuning in real-world environments, and applying these techniques to industrial automation, we can unlock the full potential of autonomous systems, making them more reliable, cost-effective, and versatile. We delve into the world of sim-to-real, exploring how simulations are used to bridge the gap between virtual testing and real-world scenarios for autonomous vehicles. Accelerating Innovation: Advantages And Potential Disruptions ### Sim-To-Real – Bridging The Gap Between Simulation And Reality Simulation has long been a valuable tool for industries ranging from automotive to robotics, allowing engineers and developers to test their designs and algorithms in a controlled and virtual environment. ### Enabling Faster Prototyping And Testing Sim-to-real technologies enable faster prototyping and testing through the following means: * Simulation provides a safe and controlled environment for testing complex algorithms and designs, ensuring that they function as intended before being implemented in the real world.

results.title: NSF funding to reduce real-to-sim gap for AI-enabled robotics
results.content: College of Engineering - University of Wisconsin Madison. autonomous research testbed (ART) software framework. # NSF funding to reduce real-to-sim gap for AI-enabled robotics. Mechanical Engineering faculty Dan Negrut recently received a four year NSF award for the project ‘Collaborative Research: Differentiable and Expressive Simulators for Designing AI-enabled Robots.’ Negrut is the Bernard A. Weideman Professor of Mechanical Engineering and co-Principal Investigator on this project with colleague Karen Liu from Stanford University. This project produces knowledge and establishes algorithms that enable computer simulation to reduce design time and costs in engineering intelligent and safe robots. This award supports fundamental research to reduce, and whenever possible eliminate, the sim-to-real gap, unlocking the full potential of AI-enabled robots. The project also advances the state of the art in robotic technologies and broaden the participation in computing of high-school students from underrepresented groups. This project is supported by the cross-directorate Foundational Research in Robotics program, jointly managed and funded by the Directorates for Engineering (ENG) and Computer and Information Science and Engineering (CISE). Special thanks to students Asher Elmquist and Aaron Young, who laid the groundwork for this simulation-in-robotics NSF project. Asher will be graduating this semester with a PhD, and Aaron has been admitted this year into the PhD program at MIT. The project period is September 2022 – August 2026. The total project award is $0.94 million, with UW-Madison receiving $423,000. autonomous research testbed (ART) software framework. *The autonomous research testbed (ART) is a software framework and 1/6th scale physical vehicle that allows the study of simulation in robotics by allowing the same autonomy algorithms to control the physical ART vehicle (top left) and the digital ART vehicle (dART – top right). The dynamics and the sensors on the vehicle are modeled in simulation, using Project Chrono, to provide synthetic data streams that mimic those provided by the real vehicle. To further facilitate the comparison between simulation and reality, real scenarios (e.g. lower left) can be replicated in simulation (lower right), to understand where simulation can be improved to better predict reality.
